issues.legal_issue: Failure to provide the accused with genuine statements recorded during the investigation does not by itself invalidate a criminal trial or require the conviction to be set aside; the consequence depends on whether the failure caused prejudice.
material_facts: The investigating officer made notes or jottings of witness statements, destroyed them, and had another officer prepare detailed statements in the witnesses’ absence.

Copies of the later-prepared statements were supplied to the accused, but they were not the statements actually recorded by the investigating officer and could not properly be used to contradict the witnesses.

The accused relied generally on the failure to supply the genuine notes, but did not raise prejudice in the High Court or advance a substantial argument showing how the failure prejudiced the defence.
The discrepancies identified in the supplied statements principally concerned persons not charged and matters of limited importance; the Supreme Court examined the evidence and found no prejudice.
issues.conclusion: The breach of the provisions governing the recording and supply of witness statements did not, on these facts, make the trial illegal or require the conviction to be set aside, because the Court was satisfied that no prejudice had resulted.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 161(3), 162, 173(4), and 207A(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 provide for recording statements, using them in limited circumstances to contradict witnesses, and supplying relevant copies to the accused. Section 537 prevents reversal for an error or irregularity unless it has occasioned a failure of justice. Narayan Rao v. State of Andhra Pradesh holds that noncompliance with the document-supply provisions is an irregularity and that proceedings may be reopened where prejudice is shown. Pulukuri Kotayya v. Emperor recognizes the value of the accused’s right to use prior statements and the possibility of inferring prejudice, while requiring the circumstances of the particular case to be considered. The Court disapproved the contrary approach in Baliram v. Emperor and Maganlal v. Emperor, and noted the case-specific approach in Maroti Mahagoo v. Emperor.

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding was a criminal trial in which the accused faced prosecution evidence.
predicates.investigation_statements_not_properly_su: The investigating officer’s actual recorded statements were not supplied to the accused for use in the defence.
predicates.court_satisfied_no_prejudice: The court, considering how the case was conducted and the accused’s response to the defect, was satisfied that the defect did not prejudice the defence.
predicates.conviction_may_be_maintained: The conviction is not set aside solely because the investigation statements were not properly supplied.

issues.definition: When a criminal trial involves failure to supply the investigating officer’s actual recorded statements, the conviction may be maintained if the court is satisfied that the failure caused no prejudice.

issues.legal_issue: A reviewing court may reverse an acquittal after reviewing the evidence, while giving proper weight to the trial court’s assessment and the accused’s presumption of innocence; a reversal is supported where the evidence establishes guilt despite the grounds on which the trial court rejected it.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused, relying on concerns including the reliability of the witnesses, the absence of independent witnesses, discrepancies about the shooting distance, and the prosecution’s inclusion of persons who were not present.

The High Court, in the prosecution’s appeal from the acquittal, relied on the testimony of eyewitnesses, including witnesses whose injuries were consistent in timing with the assault, and on supporting medical and other witness evidence.
The High Court did not rely on the testimony of the informant whose naming of absent persons had been criticized.
The trial judge’s conclusion was not founded on witness demeanour, apart from possibly the informant, and the injuries of the four witnesses supported their presence at the scene.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court found no substantial infirmity in the High Court’s assessment and declined to disturb its decision to set aside the acquittal and convict the accused.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 417, 418, and 423 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, an appellate court hearing an appeal against acquittal has power to review the evidence and reverse the acquittal. Sheo Swarup v. King Emperor requires the appellate court to give proper weight to the trial judge’s views on credibility, the presumption of innocence, the accused’s entitlement to the benefit of doubt, and the advantage of the trial judge having seen the witnesses.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The reviewing court considered an appeal seeking reversal of an acquittal.
predicates.injured_witnesses_corrobated_by_medical_: Witnesses who testified to the incident had injuries whose medical evidence supported their presence at the time and place of the incident.
predicates.trial_court_rejection_not_based_on_demea: The trial court’s rejection of the relevant testimony rested on its assessment of the evidence rather than its observation of witness demeanour.
predicates.appellate_assessment_has_no_substantial_: The appellate court’s evaluation of the evidence disclosed no substantial flaw in its reasoning.
predicates.appellate_conviction_may_be_upheld: The reviewing court may leave in place the appellate court’s decision to reverse the acquittal and convict.

issues.definition: In an appeal against acquittal, an appellate conviction may be upheld when injured witnesses are medically corroborated, the trial court’s rejection was not based on demeanour, and the appellate assessment has no substantial infirmity.
